clue.text: Primal mess sorted by little old lady in St Mary Mead

definitions.text: little old lady in St Mary Mead

indicators.note: letters that are sorted are put into a new order, so the two words before it are rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone tidies up an awful mess, helped by an elderly lady from a sleepy village.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sorted' rearranges PRIMAL MESS. St Mary Mead is the English village where Agatha Christie's elderly amateur sleuth lives.
explanation.definitionFit: Agatha Christie's spinster detective lives in the village of St Mary Mead and is famously small, elderly and sharp-eyed.

clue.text: Fowles used a novel approach to one such

definitions.text: Fowles used a novel approach to one such

parts.words: Fowles used a novel approach to one such
parts.note: John Fowles wrote a novel titled after a single wise man or sorcerer; the clue asks for that word in the plural, 'one such' being one of a group

explanation.surface: An author tried an original technique on some kind of subject.
explanation.walkthrough: 'novel approach' sounds like an innovative method, but it means Fowles wrote a novel about one of these: The Magus (1965). The answer is the plural of that title word.
explanation.definitionFit: A magus is a sorcerer or wise man, the subject of Fowles's novel; the plural form names a group of such sages.

clue.text: Novelist for whom Miss Smilla had a feeling?

definitions.meaning: C. P. ..., the English writer of the Strangers and Brothers novel sequence

definitions.text: for whom Miss Smilla had a feeling?
definitions.meaning: Peter Hoeg's thriller is titled Miss Smilla's Feeling for ... (frozen precipitation)

explanation.definitionFit: C. P. Snow was a British novelist, and Hoeg's Danish heroine has an instinct for winter flakes and ice in the book's English title.

clue.text: Relics like Plomer's Susannah Mount and Toby d'Arfey

definitions.meaning: old objects kept for display, or old-fashioned people

definitions.text: like Plomer's Susannah Mount and Toby d'Arfey
definitions.meaning: William Plomer's 1952 novel about a mother and son, Susannah Mount and Toby d'Arfey, is titled with this phrase

explanation.definitionFit: Exhibits in a gallery of antiquities are relics, and Plomer's novel calls its two antiquated characters by that phrase.

clue.text: "Thar ain't no sense / In gittin' —— "(Bret Harte)

definitions.text: "Thar ain't no sense / In gittin' —— "(Bret Harte)

parts.words: "Thar ain't no sense / In gittin' —— "(Bret Harte)
parts.note: a quotation with a gap: the missing dialect word, from Bret Harte's comic poem The Society upon the Stanislaus, means angry or annoyed

explanation.surface: A line of folksy Western verse advising calm.
explanation.walkthrough: Fill the blank in Bret Harte's line: 'there ain't no sense in getting' annoyed.
explanation.definitionFit: The missing word means angered or irritated, completing Harte's advice to keep one's temper.

clue.text: Notorious, like Chaucer's account of Good Women

definitions.text: like Chaucer's account of Good Women
definitions.meaning: Chaucer's poem is The Legend of Good Women, so it is the stuff of legend

explanation.definitionFit: Something famous enough to be talked of everywhere is the stuff of myth, and Chaucer's poem is a 'Legend'.

clue.text: Hit — and make-up

explanation.definitionFit: A smack with the palm, and actors' informal word for greasepaint, are both this short word.

clue.text: Harpo (out of control) confused with strange light in print

indicators.note: confused says the two jumbled names are mixed together into one new arrangement
something out of control runs wild, so the name before it is jumbled
strange suggests something odd or altered, so the word after it is rearranged

explanation.surface: A wild Marx brother gets tangled up with some weird lighting in a printing shop.
explanation.walkthrough: Three anagram signals: 'out of control' and 'strange' each scramble their word, and 'confused' mixes HARPO and LIGHT together. Harpo is the silent Marx brother.
explanation.definitionFit: A lithograph is a print made from a flat stone or metal plate, an artist's printed image.

clue.text: A capital girl,

parts.note: 'capital' reads as old slang for splendid, but it means a girl from France's capital city

explanation.walkthrough: 'capital' looks like the old praise word 'excellent'; here it is the capital city, Paris.
explanation.definitionFit: A woman or girl native to Paris, France's chief city, is called by this French feminine noun.

clue.text: Linguistics of comment on Ring record (unknown quantity)

parts.note: a gloss is an explanatory comment on a text
O is ring-shaped
a log is a written record, as of a voyage
y is a standard algebraic unknown

explanation.surface: Some scholarly remark about a Wagner opera cycle recording, of uncertain size.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ring' tempts as Wagner's operas, but is just the letter O.
explanation.definitionFit: Glossology is an old term for the science of language, the study of words and their meanings.

clue.text: Dennis Wheatley's was ill-omened

parts.note: The clue asks for the thing that was ill-omened in that title

explanation.surface: A comment that a thriller writer's something was unlucky.
explanation.walkthrough: The title is Star of Ill-Omen, so the clue wants its first word.
explanation.definitionFit: Wheatley's novel title names a heavenly body as the bearer of bad luck.

clue.text: Anastasia, "fair, aquiline nosed and fingered

parts.note: Dickens introduces the wife of the nouveau-riche host in Our Mutual Friend as fair, aquiline-nosed and -fingered; her first name is Anastasia

explanation.surface: A description of a pale, hawk-nosed woman called Anastasia.
explanation.walkthrough: The quotation is from Dickens's Our Mutual Friend, describing the wife of the socially climbing Hamilton Veneering, whose surname means a thin showy surface.
explanation.definitionFit: Dickens's Anastasia is the wife of the newly rich Veneering, described with exactly these features.

clue.text: Declining German family upset red Bund in written works

indicators.note: in says the rearranged letters go inside the word for written works

parts.note: books are written works

indicators.note: upset means knocked over or disturbed, so the letters of the two words before it are rearranged

explanation.surface: A German dynasty in decline overturns a red political league in its writings.
explanation.walkthrough: 'upset' scrambles 'red Bund', and 'in' puts the result inside the written works. 'Declining' is Mann's subtitle, The Decline of a Family, not the grammar sense.
explanation.definitionFit: Thomas Mann's novel charts the decay of a Lübeck merchant dynasty over four generations, its subtitle being 'The Decline of a Family'.

clue.text: Loo object as Amis subject? ( )

parts.note: jakes is an old word for a lavatory
a thing is an object

explanation.surface: Asking whether a toilet item could be a subject for a novelist.
explanation.walkthrough: Kingsley Amis wrote Jake's Thing (1978); its title, read as two words, gives a lavatory plus an object. Loo is British slang for toilet.
explanation.definitionFit: Kingsley Amis's 1978 novel is titled thus, so it is the topic of an Amis book; the question mark flags the title.

clue.text: "——!' cried Marianne,'there has been no —— *"(Sense and Sensibility)

definitions.text: "——!' cried Marianne,'there has been no —— *"(Sense and Sensibility)

parts.words: "——!' cried Marianne,'there has been no —— *"(Sense and Sensibility)
parts.note: a quotation from Jane Austen with the same word missing twice: Marianne Dashwood denies there was any betrothal or promise of marriage

explanation.surface: An outburst from an Austen heroine about something that never happened.
explanation.walkthrough: Fill both blanks with the same word: Marianne insists she and Willoughby were never formally betrothed.
explanation.definitionFit: The missing word means a formal promise to marry, which Marianne denies having had with Willoughby.

clue.text: Peak of Maurice Herzog's achievement

parts.note: 'peak' reads as high point, but it is the Himalayan mountain the French climber Maurice Herzog first summited in 1950 and wrote a book about

explanation.surface: The high point of a mountaineer's career.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Peak' looks like 'pinnacle of'; it is literally a mountain, the first 8,000-metre peak climbed.
explanation.definitionFit: Herzog's expedition made the first ascent of this Himalayan summit in Nepal, and his account bears its name.

clue.text: True fable might be deniable

indicators.note: might be signals the letters could be reshaped into something else

explanation.surface: Even a genuine story could be denied.
explanation.walkthrough: 'might be' rearranges TRUE FABLE.
explanation.definitionFit: Something that can be proved false or contradicted is open to denial.

clue.text: Successful French novelist, never in difficulty

indicators.note: something in difficulty is in a mess, so the letters of the word before it are disordered

explanation.surface: A best-selling French writer who never got into trouble.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in difficulty' scrambles NEVER.
explanation.definitionFit: Jules Verne, author of Around the World in Eighty Days, was a hugely popular French novelist.

clue.text: Eliminate artists, English from start to finish

indicators.note: says the abbreviation for English sits at both the start and the finish, with the artists between

parts.note: E is the abbreviation for English, here used at both ends
RAs are Royal Academicians, painters

explanation.surface: Get rid of the painters, the English ones, completely.
explanation.walkthrough: 'from start to finish' puts E at each end of RAS. RA is a member of Britain's Royal Academy of Arts.
explanation.definitionFit: To erase is to wipe out or remove, so eliminate is a synonym.

clue.text: "… put men into the — — of your words and make them pop like chestnuts" (Flaubert) (63)

definitions.text: "… put men into the — — of your words and make them pop like chestnuts" (Flaubert) (63)

parts.words: "… put men into the — — of your words and make them pop like chestnuts" (Flaubert) (63)
parts.note: a Flaubert quotation with a two-word gap: the kitchen utensil in which chestnuts are roasted until they pop

explanation.surface: A Flaubert line on making words roast people until they burst.
explanation.walkthrough: The gap is the pan chestnuts are roasted in; the stray '(63)' is a printing slip for the count (6,3).
explanation.definitionFit: Chestnuts are roasted over a fire in this shallow long-handled cooking vessel until they pop.

clue.text: Murdoch title as reported by Xenophon

definitions.meaning: Iris Murdoch's 1978 Booker-winning novel has a repeated title
in Xenophon's Anabasis the retreating Greek soldiers, sighting the Black Sea, shouted 'Thalatta! Thalatta!'

explanation.definitionFit: Murdoch's novel takes its name from the Greek soldiers' joyful repeated cry on seeing salt water, recorded by Xenophon.

clue.text: Habitually stands behind unfinished work

parts.note: reads like someone who always supports incomplete projects, but describes the painter's frame that literally stands behind a canvas in progress

explanation.surface: A loyal backer who always supports work in progress.
explanation.walkthrough: 'stands behind' sounds like 'supports' in the moral sense; the thing literally stands behind a painting being made.
explanation.definitionFit: An artist's wooden frame holds the canvas upright while the picture is being painted.

clue.text: Controversial contact seen in Lewes

parts.note: Rodin's marble sculpture of an embracing couple was displayed in Lewes, East Sussex, in 1914 and caused a scandal; 'contact' is the lips meeting

explanation.surface: A disputed meeting spotted in a Sussex town.
explanation.walkthrough: Lewes is a town in Sussex, England. Rodin's The Kiss was shown there in 1914 and judged too erotic; it returned in 1999, when an artist wrapped it in string.
explanation.definitionFit: A meeting of lips is a physical contact, and Rodin's statue of one caused uproar in Lewes.

clue.text: Violent ones may succeed violent delights, said Friar Laurence

definitions.text: Violent ones may succeed violent delights, said Friar Laurence

parts.words: Violent ones may succeed violent delights, said Friar Laurence
parts.note: in Romeo and Juliet Friar Laurence warns that 'These violent delights have violent' conclusions

explanation.surface: A friar's warning that passionate joys can be followed by something brutal.
explanation.walkthrough: The Shakespeare line is 'These violent delights have violent ends'.
explanation.definitionFit: Conclusions or finishes come after what precedes them, as the friar's line says of passionate joys.

clue.text: I have second American composer

parts.note: I've is the contraction of I have

explanation.surface: A claim to own a second US composer.
explanation.walkthrough: Charles Ives was an American modernist composer.
explanation.definitionFit: Charles Ives (1874-1954) was an innovative American composer of the Concord Sonata.

clue.text: Nationality of Coleridge's dulcimer-playing domestic…

parts.note: in Kubla Khan, Coleridge's 'damsel with a dulcimer' was an Ethiopian maid, named by the old word for her country

explanation.surface: Asking where a poem's musical servant girl came from.
explanation.walkthrough: Kubla Khan: 'It was an Abyssinian maid, / And on her dulcimer she played'. 'domestic' means a maid.
explanation.definitionFit: Abyssinia was the old name for Ethiopia, the homeland of the maid in Coleridge's Kubla Khan.

clue.text: One of four to Doris Lessing's city, perhaps

definitions.text: One of four to Doris Lessing's city, perhaps

parts.words: One of four to Doris Lessing's city, perhaps
parts.note: Lessing's novel is The Four-... City, so one of its four entrances is wanted

explanation.surface: One of four ways into a novelist's town.
explanation.walkthrough: Doris Lessing's 1969 novel is The Four-Gated City.
explanation.definitionFit: A city wall's entrance is an opening, and Lessing's fictional city has four of them.

clue.text: Coinages may create gloominess

indicators.note: may create says the letters of the word after it can be made into something new

explanation.surface: Newly minted words might make people depressed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'may create' rearranges GLOOMINESS. 'Coinages' could suggest money; here it is new words.
explanation.definitionFit: A coinage is a newly invented word or expression, a fresh term added to the language.
